How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is a citizen of China. He appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) that found that he had not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted on a Convention ground if he was returned to China, or that he would be personally subjected to a risk of life, or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or risk of torture.

The Appellant respectfully requests that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and find that he is a Convention refugee. In the alternative, the Appellant respectfully requests that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal. Memorandum of Appeal
Whether the Board erred in finding that the Appellant would not have been able to leave China on his own genuine passport if wanted by the Public Security Bureau.
Whether the Board erred in finding that the Appellant staged the photographs in support of his claim.
Whether the Board erred in determining that the Appellant is not a genuine practitioner of Falun Gong.
Whether the Board failed to properly assess the corroborative evidence by engaging in inverted reasoning in dismissing the Appellant's summons, arrest notice, and church letter.
The Appellant states that he is making his refugee claim based on his political opinion and Falun Gong activities.

The Appellant describes how the town government intended to expropriate land in his village and that he was unhappy with the compensation being offered. The Appellant outlined the process he went through with officials in order to receive compensation. While in Canada in XXXX 2016, he received a notice that the agreed to compensation for his land had been altered. Unable to change this altered agreement, he decided to put up a banner on XXXX XXXX, 2016 that accused the government of cheating. He also attended a demonstration and shouted that the government was corrupt and doesn't keep its promises.

Refusing to remove the banner, police officers took him away, detained him for one day, and beat him. His mother, in learning of the arrest, passed out and died in hospital. Finding out that his mother had died, the Appellant prepared other signs reviling the government and showed these signs at his mother's funeral.

Because of allergies, the Appellant began the practice of Falun Gong in late XXXX 2015 while in XXXX. The practice of Falun Gong provided relief from his medical issues. He participated in the big Falun Gong events and studied Dafa. When the Appellant was back in China, his sister learned of his practice of Falun Gong in Canada. At his sister's urging, he went into hiding, found a smuggler, and came to Canada. The police came to his home and his sister's home on the morning of XXXX XXXX, 2016, and he was ordered to report to the Public Security Bureau (PSB) on XXXX XXXX, 2016. When he failed to report, the PSB returned on XXXX XXXX, 2016 and left a summons.
After arrival in Canada, he spoke to a fellow Falun Gong practitioner and was advised to make a refugee claim. Admissibility of Evidence Submitted on Appeal

Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected1 in the circumstances to have presented at the time of the rejection.

It is for the Appellant to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meet the requirements of section 110(4), and how that evidence relates to the Appellant.2 Application of Section 110(4)

Section 110(4) establishes a disjunctive test.3 The RAD must first consider whether the proposed new evidence arose after the rejection of the refugee claim. If it did, the evidence meets the requirements of the section. If it did not, the RAD must consider whether the evidence was reasonably available for presentation to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claims. If it was not reasonably available at that time, it meets the requirements of section 110(4). If the evidence did not arise after the rejection, and it was reasonably available, the RAD must consider whether the Appellant could reasonably have been expected, in their circumstances, to have presented the evidence to the RPD prior to the rejection of their claim. If they could not have been expected to do so, the evidence meets the requirements of the section.

If the evidence did not arise after the rejection of the claim, was reasonably available, and could reasonably have been expected, in the circumstances, to be presented to the RPD prior to the rejection of the claim, the evidence does not meet the test in section 110(4). The RAD does not have the discretion to admit such evidence.4
As the RAD understands it, section 110(4) provides the Appellant with an opportunity to present evidence that could not have been submitted to the RPD.

Section 110(4) does not provide an opportunity for the Appellant to complete a deficient record submitted to the RPD; rather, it allows for the correction of errors of fact, errors in law, or mixed errors of fact and law.5

In considering whether the evidence arose after the rejection of the claim, the RAD will not restrict its analysis to the date on the proposed new evidence. In the RAD's view, a document's "newness" cannot be tested solely by the date of its creation; what is important is the event or circumstance sought to be proved by the evidence.6 Old evidence remains old evidence, even if it is placed in a new document with a recent date. Assessment of Evidence that Meets the Requirements of Section 110(4)

Where a document meets the test in section 110(4) as discussed above, the RAD will conduct a further assessment of that evidence. While section 110(4) provides the RAD with factors to consider in assessing a document's "newness," these factors alone cannot determine the admissibility of new evidence in an appeal. To put it simply, if a document is lacking in credibility or is irrelevant, it would make little sense to admit such a document, even if it meets the test in section 110(4).

In Singh,7 the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) held that there is no valid reason the RAD cannot apply the criteria set out in Raza8 to the assessment of new evidence. While Raza predates the introduction of the IRPA's section 110(4), it is based on the nearly identical wording of section 113(a). In that case, the FCA held that new evidence should be considered for its credibility, relevance, newness, and materiality, in addition to any express statutory provisions.9 In Singh, the FCA found that the criteria from Raza are necessarily implied in the wording of section 110(4).10

Where evidence meets the test in section 110(4), the RAD will go on to assess it for credibility. While this is a factor set out in Raza, there are also other reasons to apply to it. Section 171(a.3) of the IRPA allows the RAD to receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered "credible or trustworthy in the circumstances." This provision makes it clear that, in addition to the factors in section 110(4), the RAD must consider the credibility or trustworthiness of the proposed new evidence.

Relevance is a basic condition for the admissibility of any piece of evidence.11 The RAD Rule (3)(3)(g)(iii) requires the Appellant's Memorandum to include full and detailed submissions about how any proposed new evidence "relates to the Appellant." It would be highly inefficient for the RAD to admit irrelevant evidence, and contrary to section 162(2) of the IRPA, which requires that all divisions of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) "deal with all proceedings before it as informally and quickly as the circumstances and the considerations of fairness and natural justice permit."

In addition to credibility and relevance, the factors in Raza include "newness" and "materiality." Newness is implicitly incorporated into section 110(4) and does not require additional analysis. The FCA has also found materiality to be redundant, as it is also found in section 110(6) of the IRPA, which describes when the RAD may hold an oral hearing.12

The Appellant submitted a series of photographs showing his participation in Falun Gong activities.13 The Appellant also submitted the face page of The XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2017 that showed a picture of a large gathering of Falun Gong supporters in XXXX.14 The Appellant was indicated on this page with a pink marker pen. Additional photographs of the Appellant's participation in Falun Gong activities in XXXX were presented in documentation.15 Additional photos were submitted that, according to the Memorandum of Appeal, showed his participation in an event at the XXXX XXXX in XXXX, his appearance on a video site, and attendance at a Falun Gong event on XXXX XXXX, 2017.16

The Appellant submitted an affidavit17 in which he swore to his participation in a demonstration in front of the XXXX XXXX in XXXX, where he was photographed and put on a video site. In the affidavit, he further swears that he participated in the twenty-fifth anniversary celebration of Dafa, and the birthday celebration of Master Li in XXXX. He further states that he was televised on XXXX TV in XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2017.

The new evidence presented falls within the parameters of section 110 (4) of the IRPA. With respect to the affidavit of the Appellant, there are credibility issues that will be addressed in the decision that cause the RAD not to believe the Appellant. No evidence or documentation was produced to support his participation on the twenty-fifth anniversary of Dafa, the birthday celebration of Master Li in XXXX, or that he was televised on TV in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, 2017.

The remaining pictures clearly show his continuing involvement in Falun Gong activities, but do not speak to the genuineness of his practice. These pictures will be admitted as new evidence and addressed in the RAD's findings about the genuineness of the Appellant's practice of Falun Gong.
The Appellant did not request an oral hearing and the RAD, given its findings in the decision below, finds that an oral hearing is not necessary.

The Appellant supports the approach used in Huruglica for the review of RAD appeals. The decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica18 provides guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD, to decisions of the first level administrative tribunal.

The FCA stated that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard. Pursuant to subsection 111(2)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD may refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination if it is "of the opinion" that it cannot make a decision confirming or setting aside the RPD decision without hearing the evidence presented before the RPD. For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, I have applied the standard of correctness, as per Huruglica. In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, the RAD's modified standard of reasonableness may be applied in those situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in making a particular finding, as per the decision in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB). It further indicates, that although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.
Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its assessment of the RPD's decision on the basis of the principles outlined above.

The RPD found that due to its negative credibility findings, the weight given to the Notice of Summons19 is significantly diminished. Quoting Federal Jurisprudence,20 the RPD stated that "overall credibility may affect the weight given to the documentary evidence."

The RPD also noted that the summons was a single page with black ink of the stamp. The RPD quoted NDP documentation in regards to fraudulent documentation being readily available in China.21 Also, the RPD found it not credible that the Chinese authorities would issue a notice of summons on XXXX XXXX, 2016, when they would have been aware of his exit from China on XXXX XXXX, 2016.

The Appellant submits that the Board erred by failing to independently address the corroborative documentation, namely the summons, arrest notice, and Falun Gong letters. He submits that the RPD relied on prior credibility findings to dismiss the documents. The Appellant refers to documentation submitted22 that independently or in totality collaborate his claim. He submits that this constitutes a reviewable error. The Appellant referenced Federal Jurisprudence to support this submission.23

The Appellant submitted further Federal Jurisprudence to support the submission that, "the presumption of authenticity afforded to foreign documents is well entrenched in Federal Court jurisprudence."24 As a result of the above, the Appellant submitted that the RPD was obligated to apply the presumption of truthfulness to his documents, especially the Notice of Summons. He further submits, that if this had been taken into consideration, the RPD would've reached a different result and found that he will be persecuted upon return to China.

A public security summons (zhi'an chuanhuan), referenced above, was submitted in documentation to verify that the Appellant was wanted by the Chinese authorities. In observing the NDP documentation,25 the RAD notes the following: "there has been no variation in the format of summonses and subpoenas since 2003 (ibid. 22 June 2013)." The documentation goes on to quote that such forms are supposed to be used throughout the country and that "'regional variations are not meant to exist' (ibid. 24 June 2013)." Observing the summons submitted in documentation and comparing it to the samples in the NDP documentation,26 the RAD finds that the structure and format of the summons is not consistent with the documentation.

The identifier to name the individual concerned (top left) is missing. The structure of the second and third lines are inconsistent with the NDP documentation, specifically, the caricature before the number 30 is on the second line not the third. In observing the spacing and structure for the bottom three lines of the document, it is inconsistent with the documentation provided in the NDP.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the summons submitted is fraudulent; this draws a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility in submitting a fraudulent document to support his case.

Given this fraudulent documentation, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not wanted by the PSB or the authorities in China as alleged. Given that there is no credible documentation given to support his allegations of being wanted by the authorities, the RAD finds that the Appellant is not a credible witness and finds a determinative issue of his claim, i.e. being wanted by the authorities in China for his alleged practice of Falun Gong, is not credible. Given this finding, the RAD finds that the Appellant could have left China on his own documentation without difficulty and that the allegation that he used a smuggler is not credible.

As a result, the RAD will not deal with the RPD's decision or the Memorandum of Appeal issue of exiting China on his own documentation. In observing the Appellants passport,27 the RAD finds that the Appellant has traveled extensively without any apparent difficulty, and has presented no probative documentation to support that he could not have left China using his own genuine travel documents. In addition, as stated above, no additional documentation has been presented to support that he is wanted by the PSB or any Chinese authority. Given the Appellant's allegations, it would be reasonable and credible that additional documentation would have been forthcoming from the authorities if in fact he was wanted for the practice of Falun Gong in China. Genuineness of Practice of Falun Gong

The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellants ability to articulate basic facts of Falun Gong was insufficient to establish that he is a genuine practitioner, or that he would practice Falun Gong in China.. The RPD reasoned that this knowledge has to be weighed against the negative credibility findings made by the RPD. The RPD also stated that non genuine practitioners can learn the practice through memorization in a short period of time.

The RPD referenced photographs showing the Appellant distributing flyers about Falun Gong, practicing Falun Gong at XXXX XXXX XXXX and participating in a birthday celebration for Master Li on XXXX XXXX, 2015.28 The Appellant also provided a copy of his tickets to the XXXX XXXX Symphony Orchestra,29 and several letters from co-practitioners.30 The RPD found that the letters were neither sworn nor affirmed. The RPD quoted Federal Jurisprudence31 to state that negative credibility findings can be imported into an assessment of an application of a Sur Place claim. The RPD stated that since they made negative credibility findings, it can import these findings into the assessment of the Appellant's claim. As a result, the RPD placed little weight on the photographs, letters, and Symphony Orchestra ticket.

The Appellant submitted that the RPD used inverted reasoning to impugn the credibility of the Appellant. He submitted that the previous negative credibility findings do not confirm the determination as to whether the Appellant is truly a Falun Gong practitioner. The Appellant submitted that the board must make a determination on the totality of the evidence, and documents should be assessed independently of its previous credibility findings.

The Appellant submits that the RPD simply went through the motions asking questions and did not ask more complicated questions about his beliefs. He further submits that the RPD was in the position to ask more detailed questions that went beyond the scope of memorization, but did not. He further submits that the Counsel for the Appellant could not determine what level of knowledge was acceptable and that the RPD should have advised Counsel that the questions responded to were insufficient to establish more than a superficial understanding of the religion.

With regards to the photographs, letters, and orchestra ticket, the RPD provided no other reason for discounting these documents aside from its prior credibility concerns. Referring to Federal Jurisprudence,32 the Appellant submits that the letters should have been taken into consideration and remain reliable, trustworthy, and probative evidence. He submits that the Board erred in its assessment of the Falun Gong evidence, and the decision ought to be sent back for re-determination.

Given the RAD findings that the Appellant was not wanted by the Chinese authorities as alleged, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's allegations that his practice of Falun Gong in Canada was discovered by the PSB are not credible. In testimony, the Appellant stated that he had not practiced Falun Gong in any other country besides Canada. However, in further testimony, he showed an inconsistency when he testified that when he returned to China he practiced Falun Gong on his own in his home.

The RAD will assess the documents presented by the Appellant to support that he is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. In observing the photographs, referenced above, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that they do not provide proof that the Appellant is a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. The photographs show that he has been involved in Falun Gong activities, and nothing more.

The letters submitted, referenced above, are not affirmed nor were sworn. In addition, there is no indication of the expertise that each of these individuals possesses with regards to the practice of Falun Gong or their ability to determine a genuine practitioner from a non-genuine practitioner. The RAD gives these letters no weight in determining the genuineness of the Appellants practice of Falun Gong. The Symphony Orchestra ticket does not indicate the genuineness of the Appellant's practice. It simply indicates that he attended a concert, a concert open to the general public, not just Falun Gong practitioners. The RAD also finds that the new photographs and evidence accepted as new evidence cannot confirm the genuineness of practice of the Appellant. The documentation confirms that he continues to be participate in Falun Gong activities.

In listening to the recording of the RPD hearing, the RAD is aware of Federal Court's Jurisprudence which cautions against determining religious identity on the basis of a refugee Appellant's religious knowledge, or lack thereof. However, it is also important for the RAD to consider the nature of the religion or practice. It may be that some religions place little value on knowledge, and it would thus be an error to expect their adherents to value knowledge, when their belief system does not see it as important. However, objective evidence establishes that knowledge is an important component of Falun Gong (also referred to as Falun Dafa): "The foundation of Falun Dafa consists of a body of fundamental knowledge essential for the task of undertaking proper cultivation towards higher stages of attainment. It comprises Master Li's teachings collected in a number of books, the most important of which being Zhuan Falun (Revolving the Law Wheel); and China Falun Gong is a good summary of principle and exercise recommended for the beginners. Much of the teachings are highly classified knowledge that are hitherto imparted exclusively from master to trusted disciples since antiquity in China."33

As the foundation of Falun Gong is a body of fundamental knowledge, essential for the task of undertaking proper cultivation, it would be rather difficult for a purported Falun Gong practitioner to have little of this fundamental knowledge. In the RAD's view, the Appellant who claims to adhere to a knowledge-based practice may well be different than the expectations of someone who claims to follow a faith-based belief system. While this does not justify a microscopic analysis of an Appellant's evidence, it does create the expectation that the Appellant who purports to be a Falun Gong practitioner be able to testify to that essential fundamental knowledge.

The Appellant was asked to explain an attachment, a major focal point in Master Li's teachings in Zhuan Falun. He responded that it was a thought, an incorrect response. Master Li in Talk Four of Zhuan Falun talks about the process of cultivation in loss and gain. The loss that he refers to has to do with attachments and the process of eliminating unnecessary attachments. He further testified that it produced Karma, another incorrect response. He also testified that the main process in Falun Gong was getting rid of attachments, another incorrect statement. Falun Gong, as stated in documentation above, is the acquisition of fundamental knowledge for the purpose of undertaking proper cultivation towards higher stages of attainment. When asked to give examples, he stated asking for a raise in pay and smoking. In Talk Four of Zhuan Falun, Master Li talks at length about attachments, such as competitiveness, showing off, jealousy, being overjoyed, and others, and explains through the use of his philosophy how these attachments can be ameliorated through the study of Fa. The RAD finds that the appellant does not have a basic understanding of one of the main principles/processes of Falun Gong.

The Appellant knew that the Zhuan Falun is divided into nine sections. When asked what information was included in Talk Four, he testified that it talked about Loss and Gain, karma, and the emblem of Falun Gong. He then changed his testimony to state that karma was talked about in the first talk, an incorrect statement. Talk Four also talks about Improving Character, Buddhist Anointment, and Placement of the Mysterious Past. There is no discussion or picture of the Falun Gong emblem in Talk Four. In continuing testimony, the Appellant stated that Master Li talks about evil cultivation in chapter 4, an incorrect statement. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's knowledge of this chapter is deficient, and that it is not credible that he would not know this chapter given that he has read Zhuan Falun twice since October 2015 and alleges that he is a genuine practitioner.

When asked about, "evil cultivation," the Appellant stated that standing at a particular place could mean that it was evil. He then testified that if a person practiced in that way he might be demon possessed, an answer that did not address the question, or give a reasonable explanation of what this practice involved.

When asked about Righteous Thoughts, the Appellant testified that the purpose was to clean up your thoughts, an incorrect statement. He testified that you clean up other's thoughts, and the evil beings, the communist China government. According to documentation,34 Master Li advised that practitioners of Falun Gong living outside China continue to send forth righteous thoughts "in an orderly manner until the persecution is ended." Falun Gong practitioners launched a media campaign to raise awareness about the situation in China. It describes Falun Gong practitioners' efforts to reveal the "truth" about the persecution in China as a means to "'send forth righteous thoughts' to the world." "Sending forth righteous thoughts" is a meditation ritual in Falun Gong. The practice of sending forth righteous thoughts evolved in response to the persecution of Falun Gong by the Chinese authorities. The technique is performed in addition to five other meditative qigong forms that comprise the exercise system of Falun Gong. When asked about this, the Appellant gave a partial answer, but failed to describe the main purpose. According to Master Li, Righteous Thoughts are to be performed as a means of making the world aware of the persecution of Falun Gong practitioners in China.
The Appellant knew that karma was a black substance and that a white substance was virtue.

In response to the Appellant's submissions regarding the RPD's finding that more complicated questions could have been asked, the RAD finds that Counsel did not ask the Appellant any further questions about the philosophy or specific practices that he employed. Questions were asked about what Falun Gong meant to him as a practitioner, and whether he would give up Falun Gong if he went to China. In reviewing the responses above, the RAD has found that the Appellant does not demonstrate the expected knowledge of Falun Gong for one who has allegedly studied and practiced since XXXX 2015. The Appellant asked to do exercise five, and the RPD agreed. No findings were made by the RPD on this demonstration, nor did the Appellant include the performance of this exercise in his submissions. As a result, the RAD is unable to comment on this performance, but comments that this exercise is expected to be one hour in length. No comments were made by the Appellant to indicate the length of this exercise, nor did the performance of this exercise take one hour, according to the RPD hearing recording. Given the above, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is not a genuine Falun Gong practitioner. Additional Photographs

The Appellant submitted a number of additional photographs and an affidavit, referenced above under New Evidence for the RAD appeal, in order to further substantiate his allegations that he was a Falun Gong practitioner. The Appellant submits that he did practice Falun Gong in China and is wanted by the PSB. He further submits that his continued public practice of Falun Gong in Canada has made him a likely target of the PSB.

The Appellant submits, referencing NDP documentation,35 that the PSB actively monitors Falun Gong activities in Canada. He submits that the photographs and article submitted support a Sur Place claim and that public Falun Gong activities in Canada have placed him at serious risk of harm.

As stated above, the Appellant submits that the RPD erred by not considering the plethora of documentation submitted to corroborate his claim. He listed the documentation.36 The Appellant also referenced Federal Jurisprudence37 to support this submission.

With respect to the submissions made regarding the Appellant being wanted by the PSB, the RAD has found them not credible because of the fraudulent documentation. In referencing the Appellant's Basis of Claim (BOC) narrative,38 there is no indication that he practiced Falun Gong in China. He stated that his sister found out about his practice in Canada and urged him to leave China as soon as possible. As noted above, the Appellant stated he did not practice Falun Gong in China, and then changed that testimony to indicate that he had studied it at home on his own. The RPD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did not practice Falun Gong in China as alleged in his submissions.

As stated earlier, the RAD finds that the submission of this additional new evidence does not support, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant is a genuine practitioner. The photographs show that he has participated in Falun Gong activities; evidence that was available before the RPD.

With respect to his affidavit, the RAD gives no weight to the document. The RAD found the Appellant not credible when he submitted a fraudulent document indicating that he was wanted for arrest by the PSB. As a result of the submission of this document, the RAD finds that his allegations with respect to Falun Gong are not credible.

The RAD, as stated above, has reviewed the documentation submitted and addressed the particular ones that are pertinent to this decision. The RAD agrees with the Appellant in that the RPD erred by finding that the documentation submitted was fraudulent without doing an independent assessment. However, the RAD has undertaken this assessment and made findings. Although the RPD erred, the RAD will not overturn the decision based on its own findings of the documentation submitted.

No additional documentation was presented to support that the Chinese authorities are aware of the Appellant's alleged involvement in Falun Gong activities in Canada. It would be reasonable that the Chinese authorities would have made efforts to have the Appellant return if his allegations were credible. The RAD finds that the Appellant can return to China without fear of persecution from the Chinese authorities for his alleged practice of Falun Gong.

The RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal according to subsection 111(1)(a) of the IRPA. The RAD finds that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) "Robert S. Garner" Robert S.
